title: 2. The data lake
summary: From Hadoop clusters with HDFS and Hive to cloud object-store lakes: schema-on-read, cheap storage, the data swamp, and why table formats had to be invented.

blocks.text: 38.1 Context and the problem it solved

Around 2006 to 2012, web companies were producing data that did not fit the EDW: clickstream logs, server logs, sensor readings, JSON from APIs, images. Volumes were in terabytes per day, structure changed weekly, and much of the value was unknown at collection time. Loading this into a Teradata box meant designing a schema up front and paying appliance prices per terabyte.

Hadoop, based on Google's GFS and MapReduce papers, offered a different deal: a distributed file system (HDFS) on commodity servers with local disks, and a compute framework that moved code to the data. Storage cost per terabyte dropped by roughly an order of magnitude compared with appliances. The guiding idea became **schema-on-read**: store bytes as they arrive, and apply a schema only when a job or query reads them.

items: **Cheap retention**: keep raw history for years, so new questions can be answered from old data.
**Any shape**: logs, CSV, JSON, Avro, images, all in one storage system.
**Many engines**: MapReduce, then Hive, Pig, Spark, Impala, Presto over the same files.

blocks.caption: The architecture is a stack of independent layers, joined only by directory conventions and the Hive Metastore.

blocks.text: Reading bottom up: **storage** is a file system (HDFS) or an object store. **Files** are written by ingestion jobs, ideally in a columnar format such as Parquet or ORC (chapter 3). **Zones** are just directory prefixes such as `/raw/`, `/clean/` and `/curated/`; nothing enforces them. The **Hive Metastore** maps a table name to a directory, a schema and a list of partitions, which lets SQL engines treat a directory as a table. **Engines** read the files directly; there is no server that owns the data.
38.3 Components and technology choices

head: Layer
Component
Typical tools
rows: Distributed file system or object store
HDFS; Amazon S3, Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2, Google Cloud Storage
Sqoop, Flume, Kafka, NiFi, later Spark jobs and managed connectors
Hive Metastore, AWS Glue Data Catalog
MapReduce, Pig, Hive on Tez, Spark
Impala, Presto, Trino, Amazon Athena, Spark SQL

blocks.text: The move from HDFS to **cloud object storage** changed the cost model again. HDFS coupled storage to cluster nodes, so keeping 2 PB meant running enough servers to hold 2 PB times the replication factor (3 by default), even when no job was running. Object stores charge only for bytes stored and requests, and compute clusters can be started per job. The trade-off is that object stores are not file systems: renames are copies, listing large prefixes is slow, and per-request latency is tens of milliseconds (chapter 4).

**Where Iceberg, Snowflake and semantic models fit.** Iceberg was created precisely to fix the lake's table abstraction (section 38.6 and chapter 21). Snowflake sits outside a classic lake; teams typically copied curated lake data into it or later queried lake files through external tables. Semantic models were largely absent: the lake served engineers and data scientists, and governed metrics stayed in the EDW or BI tool.
38.4 Modelling and data layers in this architecture

head: Zone
Contents
Typical format and layout
rows: Exact copies of source files and events
Original format (JSON, CSV, Avro), partitioned by ingest date
Parquet or ORC, partitioned by event date

blocks.title: Hive external table over a partitioned directory (HiveQL)
blocks.text:
CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE clean.web_events (
  event_id    STRING,
  user_id     BIGINT,
  event_type  STRING,
  event_ts    TIMESTAMP,
  payload     STRING
)
PARTITIONED BY (event_date STRING)
STORED AS PARQUET
LOCATION 's3a://acme-lake/clean/web_events/';

-- New directories are invisible until partitions are registered
MSCK REPAIR TABLE clean.web_events;

The `MSCK REPAIR TABLE` step shows the core weakness: the table is a directory plus a separately maintained list of partitions. If a job writes files but the partition is not registered, or registered before all files are written, readers see missing or partial data.
38.5 Ingestion, orchestration and serving

Ingestion was ELT in spirit: land first, transform later. Batch imports (Sqoop pulling tables over JDBC), log collectors (Flume, later Kafka into HDFS or S3) and file drops all wrote to the raw zone. Spark or Hive jobs then rewrote data into the cleansed and curated zones, usually by overwriting whole partitions, because files could not be updated in place.

Orchestration moved from Oozie XML workflows to Airflow DAGs (chapter 30). Serving was the weak spot: interactive engines like Impala or Presto gave seconds-to-minutes latency on well-partitioned Parquet, which was fine for analysts but rarely good enough for hundreds of concurrent dashboard users. Many organisations therefore ran a lake *and* a warehouse, copying curated data into the warehouse for BI. That two-tier pattern is what the lakehouse (chapter 42) later tried to collapse.
38.6 Strengths, weaknesses and failure modes

head: Strengths
Weaknesses
Typical failure modes
rows: Very low storage cost per terabyte, long retention
Readers see half-written partitions during overwrites
No row-level update or delete; GDPR erasure means rewriting partitions
Erasure requests handled by rewriting terabytes, or not at all
Decoupled storage and compute (on object stores)
Schema changes are not tracked; old and new files disagree
Jobs fail or silently return nulls after an upstream column rename
Raw history enables reprocessing and new use cases
Directory listing and small files hurt performance
Millions of small files from streaming ingestion; query planning takes minutes

blocks.text: The **data swamp** is the organisational failure mode: data is collected because storage is cheap, but without owners, documentation, quality checks or retention rules. After a few years the lake holds petabytes, of which a small fraction is used, and analysts do not trust any of it. The fix is not technical alone; it needs ownership and contracts (chapters 33, 34).

The technical failure modes share one root cause: **a table was defined as 'all the files in a directory'**. Netflix created Iceberg (and Uber, Hudi; Databricks, Delta Lake) to replace that definition with an explicit list of files tracked in metadata and swapped atomically at commit. That one change gives atomic commits, snapshot isolation, schema evolution by column id, row-level deletes and hidden partitioning (chapters 21 to 23).
38.7 When to choose it / when not

items: **Choose a plain lake** for a raw archive of files that are written once and read by batch jobs: logs, images, documents, ML training corpora.
**Choose a table format on top** as soon as data is updated, deleted, read concurrently with writes, or queried with SQL by many users.
**Avoid it** as the only serving layer for governed BI with high concurrency.
**Avoid it** without a catalog, owners and retention policies; otherwise you are building a swamp.
**If you run a Hive-era lake**, migrate hot tables to Iceberg in place (metadata-only migration is often possible; check your engine's documentation) and leave cold archives as files.

blocks.title: A media company's swamp and recovery
blocks.text: A streaming media company ran a 3 PB Hadoop cluster with 40,000 Hive tables. A survey of query logs found that under 5 percent of tables had been read in the last 90 days, and that three different 'daily active users' tables existed with different numbers. Small files from hourly Flume ingestion meant some queries spent longer listing directories than reading data.
items: Moved storage to S3 and replaced the permanent cluster with per-job Spark clusters.
Deleted or archived tables with no reads and no owner after a published notice period.
Converted the 300 most-used tables to Iceberg with scheduled compaction (chapter 25).
Defined one DAU metric in the semantic layer and retired the other two tables.

blocks.title: Diagnose a lake before migrating
blocks.text: You inherit a cloud object-store lake with Hive Metastore tables, partitioned Parquet, nightly Spark overwrite jobs and a growing GDPR erasure backlog. Design an assessment: which metrics you collect (files per partition, average file size, tables by last read, schema drift incidents), how you decide which tables move to a table format first, and what governance rules you introduce so the new platform does not become a swamp again.
hints: Query logs and storage inventory reports are your main evidence.
Erasure needs and concurrent writers are strong signals for priority.
Ownership is a field in the catalog, not a wiki page.

items: The data lake traded upfront modelling and appliance cost for cheap raw storage and schema-on-read.
The Hive Metastore made directories look like tables, but a table was still 'all files in a directory'.
That definition caused partial reads, no row-level deletes, untracked schema changes and small-file problems.
The data swamp is an ownership and governance failure, not just a technical one.
Table formats such as Iceberg replaced directory listing with tracked file lists and atomic commits, turning the lake into a lakehouse.

blocks.q: What does schema-on-read mean in a data lake?
options: Readers must declare a schema before any data can be written
The query engine rewrites files into the latest schema on every read
The schema is inferred once at write time and stored with each file
Data is stored without an enforced schema and a schema is applied when it is queried
blocks.explain: Schema-on-read stores raw bytes and lets each reader apply a schema. Self-describing formats like Parquet do carry a schema, which makes "inferred once at write time and stored with each file" tempting, but the lake itself does not enforce one across files.

blocks.q: Which root cause explains most technical failure modes of a Hive-style lake?
options: Object stores cannot hold more than a few million objects
A table is defined as the set of files in a directory, with no atomic commit or file-level tracking
Spark cannot write to partitioned tables
blocks.explain: Partial reads, missing deletes and slow listing all follow from the directory-as-table definition. Parquet is columnar, and object stores scale to billions of objects, so the other options are factually wrong.

blocks.q: Why did moving from HDFS to S3 or ADLS reduce cost for many lakes?
options: Queries on object stores are faster than on local disks
Object stores support ACID transactions natively
Storage no longer required always-on compute nodes, and data was not triple-replicated on cluster disks paid for by the team
Object stores compress data better than HDFS
blocks.explain: HDFS ties storage capacity to running servers. Object stores bill for bytes and requests, and compute can be started per job. Object stores are usually slower per request than local disks, so speed was not the reason.

blocks.q: A team says 'we will avoid a data swamp by moving to Iceberg'. What is missing from this plan?
options: Ownership, documentation, quality checks and retention policies; a table format fixes table semantics, not governance
Nothing; Iceberg prevents swamps by design
Iceberg must be combined with HDFS to be governed
They should use ORC instead of Parquet
blocks.explain: Iceberg fixes atomicity, schema evolution and deletes. A swamp is caused by unowned, undocumented, untrusted data, which needs organisational controls and a catalog with owners.
